facts.title: The First Man-Made Element
facts.text: Technetium was the first element created artificially rather than discovered in nature, and its very name comes from the Greek word 'technetos', meaning 'artificial'. It was identified in 1937 by Carlo Perrier and Emilio Segrè in Palermo, Italy, after they analyzed a strip of molybdenum foil that had been bombarded with deuterons in Ernest Lawrence's cyclotron in Berkeley, California. The discovery filled a stubborn gap at atomic number 43 in the periodic table.

facts.title: Mendeleev Predicted It
facts.text: When Dmitri Mendeleev built his periodic table in 1869, he left a deliberate empty space below manganese and predicted an undiscovered element he called 'eka-manganese'. For nearly 70 years chemists hunted for it and announced several false finds, but element 43 simply does not exist in stable form on Earth. Mendeleev's prediction was finally vindicated only when Technetium was synthesized in 1937.

facts.title: Every Isotope Is Radioactive
facts.text: Technetium is the lightest element that has no stable isotopes at all; every one of its forms is radioactive. Its most stable isotope, technetium-98, has a half-life of about 4.2 million years, while technetium-97 is close behind at around 4.2 million years as well. Because these half-lives are far shorter than the age of the Earth (4.5 billion years), any technetium present when the planet formed has long since decayed away.

facts.title: A Star-Sized Clue
facts.text: In 1952 astronomer Paul Merrill detected the spectral signature of technetium in the light of certain red giant stars. Because the element's longest-lived isotopes survive only a few million years, its presence proved that these stars are actively forging new elements in their interiors right now. This was powerful, direct evidence for the theory of stellar nucleosynthesis, showing that the periodic table is still being written inside stars.

facts.title: Medicine's Workhorse Isotope
facts.text: Technetium-99m is the most widely used medical radioisotope in the world, employed in tens of millions of diagnostic scans every year. With a convenient six-hour half-life and a clean gamma-ray emission, it lets doctors image the heart, bones, kidneys, and brain with minimal radiation dose. It is conveniently 'milked' on demand from a generator containing its parent isotope, molybdenum-99.

facts.title: A Surprising Rust-Stopper
facts.text: Despite being radioactive, technetium is a remarkably effective corrosion inhibitor for steel. As little as 55 parts per million of the pertechnetate ion in water can completely protect carbon steel from rusting, even at temperatures up to 250 degrees Celsius. This property is mostly a laboratory curiosity, however, since its radioactivity rules it out for everyday use in open systems.

facts.title: It Becomes a Superconductor
facts.text: Pure technetium metal is a superconductor, losing all electrical resistance when cooled below a critical temperature of 7.46 kelvin (about minus 266 degrees Celsius). That transition temperature is unusually high among the pure elements, beaten only by a handful such as niobium and lead. The pure metal is a silvery-gray solid that slowly tarnishes in moist air.

facts.title: Born in Nuclear Reactors
facts.text: Although vanishingly rare in nature, technetium is produced in large quantities inside nuclear reactors, where it is a major product of uranium-235 fission. A typical power reactor generates roughly 27 grams of technetium-99 for every gram of fissile uranium consumed. As a result, the world's nuclear industry has accumulated many tonnes of the element, making spent fuel its primary practical source.

facts.title: Faint Traces in Earth's Crust
facts.text: Technetium is not entirely absent from nature, though it is extraordinarily scarce. Tiny amounts form continuously in uranium ores through the spontaneous fission of uranium-238, so that about one nanogram of technetium exists for every kilogram of uranium. It was first detected in African pitchblende from the Belgian Congo in 1962 by Belgian chemist Boris Kenna and Paul Kuroda.

facts.title: It Mimics Iodine in the Body
facts.text: As a member of group 7, technetium shares chemistry with manganese and rhenium and forms the pertechnetate ion, which behaves much like iodide and perchlorate in living organisms. The thyroid gland and stomach lining take it up readily, which is exactly why technetium-99m is so useful for imaging those tissues. Technetium has no natural biological role, and because it does not occur in living systems, organisms never evolved any use for it.
